q: You want to drive redundant feature weights down to exactly zero to create a sparse model. Which regularization technique should you use?
explain: L1 regularization adds an absolute value penalty which geometrically forces unimportant weights to zero. L2 shrinks weights uniformly but never eliminates them.

q: Your distance-based clustering model is yielding useless results because your features use completely different scales. What is the fix?
explain: Distance metrics like Euclidean distance are dominated by large numeric magnitudes. Standardizing or normalizing features ensures each feature contributes equally.

q: Your binary classifier is running on highly imbalanced fraud data. Why should you avoid tracking simple classification accuracy?
options: Accuracy ignores the majority class completely
Accuracy can look high by guessing the majority class
Accuracy scales poorly on small mini-batches
explain: If 99% of data is non-fraud, a broken model guessing 'no fraud' achieves 99% accuracy while catching zero fraud cases. Use F1-score instead.

q: You are training a model on tabular data with 500 features but only 100 samples. What issue should you immediately prepare for?
explain: Having far more features than samples leads to data sparsity and overfitting, known as the curse of dimensionality. Reducing dimensions is necessary.

q: Your Q-learning agent is only choosing familiar paths and missing hidden, higher-value rewards. What parameter needs tuning?
explain: The agent is exploiting known paths instead of exploring new ones. Increasing the exploration rate (epsilon) forces the agent to discover alternative strategies.

q: You change your regression loss function from Mean Squared Error to Mean Absolute Error. How does this alter model behavior?
options: The model ignores small training errors
The model becomes robust to outliers
explain: Mean Squared Error squares residuals, making it hyper-sensitive to large outliers. Mean Absolute Error scales linearly, dampening outlier influence.

q: You notice your training loss bounces around violently without converging. What hyperparameter adjustments should you test first?
explain: An excessive learning rate causes optimization steps to overshoot local minima, preventing smooth convergence. Lowering it stabilizes gradient descents.

q: You decide to implement an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm that updates state-action values greedily. Which method fits this description?
explain: Q-learning is off-policy because its value update assumes greedy future actions regardless of what action the exploratory policy actually selected.

q: You want to evaluate an unsupervised anomaly detection model but have zero labeled samples. What approach should you use?
explain: Without labels, you cannot build traditional validation matrices. Tracking reconstruction error via autoencoders allows flagging high-deviation points as anomalies.

q: You are tuning a binary model for medical diagnostics where missing a disease is catastrophic. What threshold shift should you make?
options: Keep threshold at exactly point five
Zero out threshold to stop predictions
explain: Lowering the classification threshold makes the model more willing to flag positive cases. This catches more true cases, maximizing crucial recall scores.

q: Your deep network gradients drop exponentially toward zero within the early layers during backpropagation. What activation change should you consider?
explain: Saturating functions like Sigmoid compress large inputs, creating tiny derivatives. ReLU maintains a constant derivative of one for positive inputs, mitigating vanishing gradients.

q: You want to train a model to match pairs of similar unlabelled items while pushing different items far apart. What framework do you need?
explain: Contrastive learning optimizes feature extraction spaces by pulling representations of positive pairs closer together and repelling negative pairs.

q: Your cross-validation setup shows excellent training results, but validation variance fluctuates wildly across folds. What does this suggest?
options: The dataset contains high bias traits
The model is overfitting specific data splits
The learning rate is too small
The feature scaling was skipped entirely
explain: High performance variance across cross-validation folds indicates overfitting. The model is over-indexing on localized noise present within individual training splits.

q: You want to build a reinforcement learning system that directly learns action probabilities without tracking state-action tables. What category of RL is this?
explain: Policy-based methods optimize action probability distributions directly through policy gradients, completely avoiding intermediate value state calculations.

q: You have a dataset with 1,000,000 unique categorical text tokens. Why should you avoid standard one-hot encoding here?
options: It makes vectors continuous and unreadable
It creates massive, ultra-sparse memory footprints
It automatically forces linear model behavior
explain: One-hot encoding creates a vector size equal to the cardinality. For 1,000,000 items, this introduces massive sparsity and memory bloat. Use dense embeddings instead.

q: You want to ensure your cross-validation tracks the correct target class proportions within every single fold split. Which variation do you use?
explain: Stratified cross-validation preserves target class balance across all splits. This is vital when validating models on highly imbalanced datasets.

q: Your network training speed drops drastically because you process the entire dataset before updating weights once. What optimization variant are you using?
explain: Batch Gradient Descent calculates gradients over the whole dataset before a single parameter update. This demands massive computation and slows iterations down.

q: You want to implement an anomaly detection algorithm that isolates outliers by randomly branching feature values into tree nodes. What model do you pick?
explain: Isolation Forest isolates anomalies by randomly partitioning features. Outliers require fewer tree splits to isolate, resulting in noticeably shorter tree paths.

q: Your model shows an excellent balance between structural simplicity and noise sensitivity. How would you describe its position?
explain: The bias-variance tradeoff balances structural underfitting errors against noise oversensitivity. Finding the optimal sweet spot minimizes generalization error.

q: You want to reduce overfitting on your training set by explicitly balancing empirical risk against overall model complexity. What framework are you executing?
explain: Structural Risk Minimization adds a complexity penalty to empirical risk optimization. This directly restrains model capacity to guarantee better generalization bounds.

q: Your classifier outputs continuous values from negative infinity to positive infinity. What activation should you use to convert them to binary probabilities?
explain: Sigmoid compresses unbounded logits into a strict $(0, 1)$ probability range, making it ideal for standard binary classification tasks.

q: You notice your model training loss flatlines instantly, but you did not change the architecture. What training parameter might be configured wrong?
explain: If the learning rate is accidentally set to zero, gradients cannot modify weight parameters. The model stops learning completely and loss flatlines.

q: You want to measure how many true negative samples your classifier correctly identified out of all actual negative cases. What metric do you track?
explain: Specificity measures the true negative rate. It answers how many actual negative instances were correctly flagged, matching the inverse of recall.

q: Your model behaves erratically because you pass a single random training sample per weight update step. What optimizer approach are you running?
explain: Pure Stochastic Gradient Descent updates weights after processing one random sample. This speeds up steps but introduces noisy gradient trajectories.

q: You notice your deep multi-layer network is memorizing training sequences instead of extracting abstract shapes. What adjustment will help reduce model capacity?
explain: Increasing L2 regularization penalizes large weights, restricting model capacity. This forces the model to ignore noise and learn generalized features.
